items.title: Words to a rule
items.prose: A machine multiplies its input by 4, then subtracts 7.
items.question: Complete the rule $f(x) = \ldots$. Type only what comes after the $=$ sign.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply first, then subtract 7.

byKey.brackets: You wrote $4(x - 7)$, which subtracts first. For $x = 10$ the machine gives 33, but yours gives 12.

explain.text: Multiplying comes first, so no brackets are needed: $f(x) = 4x - 7$. Check with $x = 10$: $40 - 7 = 33$.

items.title: Inputs in threes
items.prose: A table gives inputs −2, 1, 4 and 7, with outputs 11, 5, −1 and −7.
items.question: What is $f(10)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the output climb by the input climb.

byKey.climb-m: You used the climb of −6 as the multiplier. The input climbs by 3, so $m = -2$.
byKey.sign: The outputs fall as the inputs rise, so the multiplier is negative.
byKey.sign2: 13 loses the sign at the last step. The line falls, so f(10) = 7 − 20, and 20 is bigger than 7, which leaves −13.

explain.text: The outputs fall 6 for each input climb of 3, so $m = -2$. Row 2: $5 = -2 \times 1 + c$, so $c = 7$. Then $f(10) = 7 - 20 = -13$.

items.title: A hollow end that does not matter
items.question: What is the range?

options.why: You used the two ends of the domain only. $x = 1$ is inside and gives 0.
The input 0 is left out, but the output 1 still comes from $x = 2$.
9 comes from $x = 4$, and 4 is in the domain: its end is filled.

feedback.correct: The outputs run from 0, at $x = 1$, to 9, at $x = 4$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the smallest and largest outputs, then check which are reached.

explain.text: The smallest output is $f(1) = 0$ and the largest is $f(4) = 9$. The hollow end at $x = 0$ removes that input, but its output 1 is reached again at $x = 2$. So the range is $0 \le f(x) \le 9$.

items.title: Splitting the input
items.prose: $f(x) = 3x - 2$. For any numbers $a$ and $b$, the expression below gives the same answer.
items.question: What is $f(a) + f(b) - f(a + b)$?

widget.label: f of a plus f of b minus f of a plus b

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write out $f(a)$, $f(b)$ and $f(a + b)$ in full first.

byKey.equal: You assumed $f(a) + f(b) = f(a + b)$. The sum subtracts 2 twice; $f(a + b)$ subtracts it once.
byKey.sign: You subtracted the wrong way round. $f(a) + f(b)$ is the smaller one.
byKey.double: You stopped at the −4 in $f(a) + f(b)$. Subtracting $f(a + b)$ takes away its −2 as well.

items.title: The worst case of a call
items.prose: You buy a call option with strike £120.00 for a premium of £4.50. The call pays the final share price minus £120.00 when the price ends above £120.00, and nothing otherwise. You pay the £4.50 premium up front, so your profit and loss is the payoff minus £4.50. The graph shows it against the final share price.
items.question: What is the lowest value in the range of the P&L, in pounds?

feedback.correct: The worst case is losing the £4.50 premium.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the lowest height of the line.

byKey.payoff: 0 is the lowest payoff. The P&L also takes off the £4.50 you paid.
byKey.strike: £120.00 is the strike, a price on the bottom axis. It is an input, not a P&L.
byKey.sign: Paying the premium is a cost, so the lowest P&L is negative.

explain.text: At any final price up to £120.00 the call pays nothing, so you are down the £4.50 premium. Above £120.00 the P&L climbs. So the range is P&L $\ge -4.5$.

lines.text: $3y = 2x + 5$, multiplying both sides by 3 undoes the divide

feedback.correct: Undo the last step first: the divide, then the add, then the doubling.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The machine doubled, added 5, then divided by 3. Undo in reverse.

explain.text: $f$ doubles, adds 5, then divides by 3. Undoing reverses the order: multiply by 3, subtract 5, divide by 2. The check confirms it: $f(2) = \tfrac{9}{3} = 3$ and $g(3) = \tfrac{4}{2} = 2$.

items.title: A fee schedule at its boundaries
items.prose: A broker charges £3.00 for trades up to and including £500.00, £7.50 for trades above £500.00 up to and including £2,500.00, and 0.4% of the trade value above £2,500.00. You place three trades: £500.00, £2,500.00 and £4,000.00.
items.question: What do the three fees add up to, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put each trade in its band, watching the words "up to and including".

byKey.boundaries-up: You moved each boundary trade into the band above. "Up to and including" keeps £500.00 and £2,500.00 in the lower bands.
byKey.percent: You used 0.4 for 0.4%. As a decimal, 0.4% is 0.004.

explain.text: £500.00 and £2,500.00 stay in their lower bands, at £3.00 and £7.50. £4,000.00 is above £2,500.00, so its fee is $0.004 \times 4000 = 16$. The total is £26.50.

items.title: Profit as a function of quantity
items.prompt:
You plan to buy $q$ shares at £18.40 and sell them later at £19.05. The broker charges £7.50 on each trade, so £15.00 for the buy and the sell together. You can trade any whole number of shares from 1 to 1,000.

(a) Write your profit $P(q)$, in pounds, as a function of $q$.

(b) Find $P(10)$, $P(100)$ and $P(1000)$.

(c) State the domain of $P$, and describe its range: its smallest value, its largest value, and whether every amount in between is possible.

(d) Find the smallest number of shares that makes a profit. Show the two values of $P$ either side.

(e) Explain whether $P$ can be undone: given a profit, can you always find the one $q$ that produced it? Write the undoing rule.
items.model:
**(a)** Each share gains $19.05 - 18.40 = 0.65$ pounds, and the fees cost £15.00 once. So $P(q) = 0.65q - 15$.

**(b)** $P(10) = 6.50 - 15 = -8.50$, a loss of £8.50. $P(100) = 65 - 15 = 50$, a profit of £50.00. $P(1000) = 650 - 15 = 635$, a profit of £635.00.

**(c)** The domain is the whole numbers $q = 1, 2, \ldots, 1000$. $P$ rises with $q$, so the smallest output is $P(1) = 0.65 - 15 = -14.35$ and the largest is $P(1000) = 635$. Not every amount between is possible: outputs go up in steps of £0.65, so for example £0.00 is never reached.

**(d)** A profit needs $0.65q - 15 > 0$, so $q > \tfrac{15}{0.65} \approx 23.08$. The smallest whole number is $q = 24$. Check either side: $P(23) = 14.95 - 15 = -0.05$, a loss of 5p, and $P(24) = 15.60 - 15 = 0.60$, a profit of 60p.

**(e)** Different $q$ give different profits, because each extra share adds £0.65. So each profit in the range comes from exactly one $q$, and $P$ can be undone. Reverse the steps: add 15, then divide by 0.65, giving $q = \dfrac{P + 15}{0.65}$. Check: a profit of £50.00 gives $q = \tfrac{65}{0.65} = 100$.

rubric.text: Writes $P(q) = 0.65q - 15$, with £0.65 per share and the £15.00 of fees charged once.
States the domain as whole numbers 1 to 1,000 and the range from −£14.35 to £635.00, in steps of £0.65 with gaps.
Explains that each profit comes from one $q$, and gives $q = \tfrac{P + 15}{0.65}$ with a check.
